evidence.claim: Idaho’s Hells Canyon Scenic Byway runs from Cambridge to the Snake River, then north along the Idaho bank toward Hells Canyon Dam.
evidence.quote: Head west from Cambridge on Highway 71 to the Oxbow Bridge near Copperfield, Oregon, then north along the Idaho side of the Snake River to Hells Canyon Dam.

evidence.claim: Highway 71 is two lanes through largely remote, sparsely populated country.
evidence.quote: SH-71 is a two-lane road for its length. Except for the area near is southern terminus, SH-71 runs through remote and very sparsely populated areas.

evidence.claim: Hells Canyon Road is narrow and winding, with several steep grades.
evidence.quote: Hells Canyon Road is a narrow, winding road with several steep grades.

evidence.claim: Three Idaho Power dams reshaped this stretch of the Snake: Brownlee, Oxbow and Hells Canyon.
evidence.quote: the Hells Canyon Project, which includes Brownlee Dam (1959) and Oxbow Dam (1961), all built and operated by Idaho Power Company.

evidence.claim: They replaced a proposal for a single 710-foot-high dam.
evidence.quote: three dams (Hells Canyon, Brownlee Dam and Oxbow Dam) taking the place of a single 710-foot (220 m) high dam.

flags: Cache 00 describes Oregon’s separate 218.4-mile All-American Road; none of its designations or dates are transferred to Idaho.

Archived Visit Idaho 2013 describes 22 miles and allows three hours; 2024 includes Cambridge and Brownlee, gives 62.4 miles and 1 hour 43 minutes. Use the broader 2024 scope; material maps only 21.9 miles in the reverse direction. Moments follow the official Cambridge-to-dam itinerary.
No construction history or designation date for Idaho’s byway is cached; the overview uses hydropower history without claiming the dams caused road construction.

The general canyon article gives dam completion years conflicting with individual dam articles; omitted disputed completion years. Salmon blockage endpoints also differ; state only the shared upstream-migration consequence.
Tourism pages are archived, so year-round maintenance, visitor-center season, tours and current access are not verified for 2026. No operational assurance or practical note supplied.

No Tribal source is cached. Tourism uses Nez Perce, Shoshone, Bannock, North Paiute and Cayuse; canyon article uses Nez Percé, Shoshone-Bannock, northern Paiute and Cayuse. Omitted specific authorship of rock art and settlement motives.
